parts.transcript: For my presentation, I’m going to summarize the findings of a research project on life aboard the International Space Station in the early days of its operation, its teething problems, as it were. I’ll start by giving a little background information. The space station crew were essentially a constantly changing team of scientists from different countries who lived on the space station for several months at a time, and they conducted a number of experiments, including some studies of living conditions in space, which is what I’m going to be looking at now. So, what was life like on board in the very confined conditions of the space station? Well, the early impressions recorded by the astronauts were very different from what people had expected. They’d expected that the air would smell stale or artificial, but the astronauts found that it was fresh, so that was one very positive finding. And although they were in such a confined space, and people worried that it would get very hot, in fact, they found that it was very easy to turn the temperature up or down in order to keep it within a comfortable range. The feedback on the food was also positive. Astronauts on previous space stations had described the meals as boring, but the International Space Station meals were praised for their variety, so that was another good piece of feedback. And something which is taken for granted today, but was a key morale booster in those days, was communication between the space station and Earth, which the astronauts said was clear and reliable. So, in the early days, it seems that the mood was overall very positive. However, after a few days, the difficulties and frustrations became clearer. Above all, the crew complained about the constant noise caused by the air filters, which used to rattle and buzz 24 hours a day, interrupting their sleep. As well as that, the astronauts complained that the Velcro fasteners, which were positioned all over the station, didn’t work well, and so a lot of the time, objects weren’t secure in the cabin but floated about. A particularly serious problem was that the systems used on the space station had been developed in a number of different countries, and they didn’t always work well together. passages.title: Passage 1: Starting school later has positive effects on teens
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Starting school later has positive effects on teens

A growing body of evidence demonstrates that adolescents benefit substantially from additional sleep. When school districts postpone the start of the academic day, measurable improvements tend to follow. With lessons that commence as early as 7 a.m. and buses that arrive well before sunrise, roughly 80 per cent of US children in grades 6 through 12 fail to obtain the recommended quantity of sleep during term time, according to research by the National Sleep Foundation, a sleep advocacy organisation. These premature start times appear to contribute to a multitude of difficulties. Exhausted children, studies indicate, not only struggle with irritability, but also with symptoms of depression. They tend to gain weight, their academic grades deteriorate, and many resort to caffeine, with dubious consequences for productivity and uncertain effects upon the development of immature brains.

Now, propelled by accumulating research suggesting that adolescents are biologically predisposed to sleep late, and that delaying school start times by even a mere 30 minutes generates a pronounced difference in how well teenagers feel and perform, an increasing number of institutions across the United States are beginning the school day later than they formerly did. Many more are deliberating the question. Simultaneously, however, there remain entrenched pockets of resistance from administrators and parents who contend that bus schedules will become excessively complicated, that a later commencement will interfere with extracurricular programmes, or that children will simply remain awake later if they realise they can sleep in somewhat longer.

According to Kyla Wahlstrom, director of the Center for Applied Research and Educational Improvement at the University of Minnesota, although the two districts she examined could not have been more different in terms of race, socioeconomic status and other factors, beneficial changes in both places became apparent almost immediately.

Several of the outcomes were notably significant. For instance, students were perceptibly more alert during the first two periods of the day. Furthermore, the cafeteria was calmer, and fewer altercations erupted in the corridors. Students, who were now obtaining nearly an additional hour of sleep each night, reported that they felt less depressed. Even parents informed teachers that they considered their children easier to live with than before.

The melatonin shift

Biology, rather than laziness, should be held responsible for adolescents’ reluctance to rise in the morning. As children mature and approach puberty, a phase of profound biological transformation, their bodies begin to circulate melatonin—the hormone that induces sleepiness—approximately two hours later than they previously did.

Consequently, teenagers find it virtually impossible to fall asleep before roughly 11 p.m., even when they make a deliberate attempt to retire earlier. Yet adolescents nonetheless require an average of 9.25 hours of slumber each night. Superimposed upon this shift in natural sleeping and waking rhythms lies a second factor: a phase of intense drowsiness that afflicts both adults and adolescents during the early-morning hours. In adults, this trough in alertness occurs between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m.; in adolescents, it descends between approximately 5 a.m. and 7 a.m. The implication is that, while their alarm clocks instruct teenagers to leave their beds and demand that their brains perform, their bodies are simultaneously signalling them to continue sleeping.

Beyond these mood, behavioural and learning consequences, scientists are progressively uncovering more subtle mechanisms through which such chronic sleep deprivation can damage children. Certain studies, for example, demonstrate that insufficient sleep compromises the immune system. Others suggest that, when sleep is inadequate, the body secretes elevated quantities of the hormones that trigger hunger, a process that may plausibly contribute to escalating rates of obesity.

In order to remain awake, young people frequently resort to coffee, soda and other caffeinated beverages. At one public high school in the eastern US state of Massachusetts, 95 per cent of the students surveyed reported consuming caffeine within the preceding fortnight—predominantly in the form of soda rather than coffee, and most commonly during the afternoon and evening hours—Dr Amy Wolfson and a colleague reported in the journal Health Education and Behavior. According to Dr Wolfson, no published guidelines currently specify how much caffeine constitutes an excessive amount for adolescents. The substance, however, persists within the body for up to five hours—three hours longer than was originally assumed—thereby depriving teenagers of an indeterminate number of hours of sleep. Even when caffeinated teenagers do manage to fall asleep, caffeine demonstrably renders the quality of that sleep worse. Finally, no one yet understands how caffeine may influence developing brains, although numerous experts remain concerned about the apparent connection between the sugar contained in soda and consequent weight gain.

Schools respond

As the body of sleep research continues to accumulate, an expanding number of schools are gravitating towards later start times. No one has formally documented precisely how many institutions have implemented the change, yet experts report that they are receiving a steadily increasing volume of enquiries from districts throughout the US, requesting advice on whether and how to adopt a later schedule. Whatever the practical obstacles, adolescents need to obtain sufficient sleep, and altering school start times has proven to be one effective means of achieving that objective.

passages.title: Passage 2: Boring Buildings
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Boring Buildings

There could be more than an economic or nostalgic price to impersonal retail and high-rise construction; boring architecture may take an emotional toll on the people forced to live with it.

A A growing body of research in cognitive science illuminates the physical and mental toll that bland cityscapes take on residents. Generally, these researchers argue that humans are healthier when they live surrounded by variety, or work in well-designed, unique spaces, rather than in unattractive, generic ones. Urban policy professor Justin Hollander and architect Ann Sussman review scientific data to help architects and urban planners understand how, exactly, people respond to their built surroundings, particularly at work. People, they argue, function best in intricate settings, not ‘big, blank, boxy offices’.

B Indeed, that is what Colin Nellard, a neuroscientist at the University of Waterloo in Canada, has found in his work. Five years ago, Nellard became interested in a certain building — the gigantic Whole Foods Market ‘plopped into’ a notoriously textured part of lower Manhattan in New York. Nellard partnered with the Guggenheim Museum to analyse what happens when someone walks out of a tiny neighbourhood restaurant and encounters a full city block with nothing but ‘the long, blank facade of the Whole Foods Market’ building.

In 2011, Nellard led small groups on Lower East Side walks to measure the effect of the urban environment on them. Participants recorded their responses to questions at each stopping point and wore sensors that measured skin conductance, a response to emotional excitement. Passing the monolithic Whole Foods Market, people’s state of arousal plummeted. Physiologically, Nellard explained, they were bored, and to describe this place they used words like ‘bland’ and ‘passionless’. In contrast, one block east at the other test site — a ‘lively sea of restaurants with lots of open doors and windows’ — people measured high levels of excitement, and they listed words like ‘lively’ and ‘socialising’. Nellard explains that the main objective of urban design should be to produce some kind of novelty or change every few seconds; otherwise, we become cognitively disengaged.

C The trick, it seems, is to design a world that excites but does not overload our faculties with a constant barrage of information. ‘We are, as animals, programmed to respond to thrill,’ said professor Brendan Walker. In Walker’s ‘thrill laboratory’ at the University of Nottingham in the UK, devices measure heart rate and skin conductance to see how people respond to adrenaline-producing experiences such as a roller-coaster ride. A thrilling encounter moves us quickly from a state of equilibrium to a desirable ‘disorientation’. ‘Humans want a certain element of turmoil or confusion,’ he said. ‘Complexity is thrilling, whether in an amusement park or in architecture.’

D Psychologists have found that awe-inspiring moments can potentially improve our well-being. One study, conducted by Melanie Rudd, Kathleen Vohs and Jennifer Aaker of Stanford University in the US, showed that the feeling of ‘awe’ can make people more patient and less materialistic. In an experiment, the researchers showed students 60-second clips of waterfalls, whales, or astronauts in space. After only a minute of these virtual images, those who said they were awed also felt less pressed for time. In another variation, people made hypothetical choices between physical and experiential goods of equal monetary value. Those who had just ‘felt awe’ were more likely to choose an experience over a possession, a choice that is linked with greater satisfaction in the long run. In other words, a visual buzz — whether architectural or natural — might have the ability to change our frame of mind, making modern-day life more satisfying and interactive.

E It is important to note, however, that architectural boredom is not about how pristine a street is. People often confuse successful architecture with whether an area looks pleasant. On the contrary, when it comes to city buildings, people often focus too narrowly on aesthetics, said Charles Montgomery, author of Happy City: Transforming Our Lives Through Urban Design. Some of the happiest blocks in New York City, he argues, are ‘kind of ugly and messy’.

In 2014, Montgomery’s Happy City lab conducted an experiment in which he found a strong correlation between messier blocks and pro-social behaviour. Montgomery sent researchers, posing as lost tourists, to places he coded as either ‘active’ or ‘inactive’ facades. He concluded that the former had a high level of interest — that is, they were messy — while the latter had no special features, such as long warehouse blocks. Pedestrians at active sites were nearly five times more likely to offer assistance than at inactive ones, and of those who assisted, seven times as many at the active site offered the use of their phone.

F Fortunately, it is not necessarily a dichotomy — new architecture can achieve the optimal level of cacophony and beauty. Take the 2006 Hearst Tower in midtown Manhattan. Designed by architect Norman Foster, Hearst Tower is a glass-and-steel skyscraper, 40 stories of which are designed in a triangular pattern, differing in style from the 1920s Art Deco base. From the outside, the facade jolts city dwellers from their daily commutes, while energising employees who enter it each morning. For many who walk by, Hearst Tower’s design may not be the easiest to understand; it is both sleek and old, and the top looks as though it travelled from the future. Inside, workers travel upon diagonal escalators, up a three-story water sculpture, through the tower’s historic atrium, flooded with light. Few New Yorkers who pass by would find this building boring — and they are likely to be happier, maybe even nicer to each other, because of it.

passages.title: Passage 3: The Communication of Science
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

The Communication of Science

Science plays an increasingly significant role in people’s lives, making the communication by journalists in the popular media of scientific developments more important than ever. Yet such communication is fraught with challenges that can easily distort discussions and lead to unnecessary confusion. Some problems stem from the esoteric nature of current research and the associated difficulty of coming up with sufficiently faithful terminology. Abstraction and complexity are not signs that a given scientific direction is wrong, but are instead a tribute to the success of human ingenuity in meeting the challenges that nature presents. They can, however, make communication more difficult.

But many of the biggest challenges for scientific reporting arise because, in areas of evolving research, scientists tend to be specialists, and often only partly realise the significance of any particular advance or development. Since that partial understanding applies to most of the scientific developments that directly affect people’s lives, such as cancer research and diet studies, learning how to overcome it is critical to stimulating a more informed scientific debate among the broader public.

Ambiguous word choices are the source of some misunderstandings. Scientists often employ common terminology, to which they then assign a specific meaning that is impossible to fathom without a precise definition. Take Einstein’s famous theory of relativity. The term ‘relativity’ here is intrinsically misleading. Many interpret the theory to mean that everything is relative and there are no absolutes. Yet although the measurements any observer makes depend on his coordinates and reference frame, according to Einstein’s theory, the physical phenomena he measures, in fact, have an invariant description that transcends that observer’s particular coordinates. The physical phenomena are not relative. Even Einstein admitted that the term relativity was probably misleading.

But not all communication problems stem solely from poor word choices. Some are inherent in the intrinsically complex nature of much of modern science. Science sometimes transcends this limitation: remarkably, chemists were able to detail the precise chemical processes involved in the destruction of the ozone layer, so the evidence that chlorofluorocarbon gases (Freon, for example) were destroying the ozone layer was successfully conveyed to the public.

How journalists report scientific developments on vital issues of the day that are less well understood, or in which the connection is less direct, is a more complicated question. Global warming patterns are a case in point. Even if we understand some effects of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, it is difficult to predict the precise chain of events that a marked increase in carbon dioxide will cause. The distillation of results presented to the public in such cases should reflect at least some of the subtleties of the most current developments.

Balanced reporting, of course, can help public understanding when there is genuine uncertainty or when competing interpretations are still strongly supported by evidence. Journalists should seek to provide opposing or competing views on controversial issues only when those views reflect a real division within the scientific community. Almost all newly discovered results will have some supporters and some opponents, and only time and further evidence will clarify the true story. However, in the global warming debate, the press often continued to present the issue as though scientists were evenly divided, even after the bulk of the scientific community had recognised the seriousness of the problem. In this case, the attempt to give equal weight to both sides did not improve public understanding; instead, it created a misleading impression of uncertainty.

A better understanding by the general public of the mathematical significance of results would help to clarify many scientific discussions. Statistical analysis can show whether particular results are significant or could occur simply by chance. A few years ago, the Harvard University faculty was tortured by empty debates over the relative intrinsic differences in the scientific abilities of men and women. One of the more amusing aspects of the discussion was that those who believed in the differences and those who didn’t used the same evidence in their opposing arguments about gender-specific scientific ability. How could that be? The answer is that the data did show gender differences, but no statistically significant differences in inherent scientific ability based on gender.

There are steps we can take to improve public understanding of scientific developments. The first would be to inculcate greater understanding and acceptance of indirect scientific evidence not directly observable by human scientists. The information from an unmanned space mission is no less legitimate than the information from one in which people are on board. Second, we might need different standards for evaluating science with urgent policy implications, as opposed to research with a purely theoretical value. Third, it would be better if scientists were more prepared to discuss the mathematical significance of their results, and if the public didn’t treat maths as quite so scary: statistics, which tell us the uncertainty in a measurement, give us the tools to evaluate new developments fully.

But fourth, and most important, people have to recognise that science can be complex. If we accept only straightforward stories, the description will necessarily be distorted. When advances are subtle or complicated, scientists should be willing to go the extra distance to give proper explanations, and the public should be more patient about the truth. Even so, some difficulties are unavoidable. Most developments reflect work in progress, so the story is complex because no one yet knows the big picture. Although the more involved story might not have the same immediate appeal, the truth in the end will always be far more interesting.

task1.title: Task 1: Report / Data Description
task1.prompt: The chart and table below show the proportion of energy generated from renewable and non-renewable sources in selected OECD countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
task1.sampleBand8Answer:
The chart and accompanying table illustrate the comparative distribution of electricity production from renewable and conventional non-renewable sources across four OECD member nations—namely Germany, Sweden, Canada, and Japan—over a twenty-year timeframe from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, it is immediately apparent that all surveyed nations witnessed an upward trajectory in green energy adoption, with Sweden maintaining the foremost position in clean energy reliance throughout. Conversely, Japan continued to exhibit the lowest proportion of renewables despite moderate progress in the final decade.

In detail, Sweden commenced the period with 42% of its total energy coming from renewables in 2000, which subsequently expanded sharply to surpass 68% by 2020, driven primarily by investments in hydroelectric and wind installations. Canada similarly sustained high renewable dependency, starting at 56% and peaking at 64% by the end of the survey period.

In contrast, Germany underwent the most dramatic structural shift: renewable output represented a modest 8% in 2000 before quadrupling to approximately 39% in 2020 under comprehensive decarbonization initiatives. Japan, by comparison, began at just 7% and grew modestly to 18% in 2020, still leaving fossil and nuclear fuels to comprise the vast majority (82%) of its energy grid.

task2.title: Task 2: Academic Essay
task2.prompt: Some people believe that artificial intelligence and automation will bring massive unemployment and economic instability. Others argue that AI will foster innovation and create higher-value jobs. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
task2.sampleBand8Answer:
The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic automation has ignited rigorous debate across global economic forums. While a considerable segment of the population expresses trepidation regarding widespread redundancy and fiscal volatility, others contend that this technological paradigm will unlock unprecedented productivity and cultivate novel vocational sectors. In my view, although transient displacement is inevitable, AI will ultimately function as a net positive catalyst for societal affluence.

On the one hand, apprehensions regarding job scarcity are grounded in historical precedent and empirical reality. In routine-intensive fields such as manufacturing, logistics, and entry-level clerical administration, autonomous algorithms execute quantitative computations and physical tasks with far greater velocity and precision than human operators. Consequently, unmitigated deployment without rigorous retraining frameworks risks marginalizing millions of low-skilled workers, thereby exacerbating wealth disparity and burdening public welfare reserves.

On the other hand, proponents persuasively assert that technological upheavals historically eliminate specific tasks rather than labor as a whole. By relieving human professionals of mundane, repetitive drudgery, automation creates capacity for higher-order cognitive domains such as ethical AI governance, specialized software architecture, and creative strategic consulting. Furthermore, empirical analyses indicate that machine-augmented industries stimulate secondary employment ecosystems—from renewable infrastructure to tailored biotechnology—which generate premium remuneration.

In conclusion, while the transition phase undeniably poses formidable challenges for specific occupational demographics, artificial intelligence represents a profound evolution rather than an existential crisis for the labor market. Governments and educational institutions must proactively orchestrate lifelong upskilling programs to ensure equitable participation in this automated era.

cueCard.prompt: Describe a memorable professional or academic achievement that you are proud of.
bullets: When and where it took place
What challenges you had to overcome
And explain why you felt so proud of this accomplishment.

part2.sampleBand8Answer:
I would like to speak about a defining professional achievement from last year, when I successfully spearheaded the migration of our company's legacy customer management infrastructure to a secure cloud platform. This undertaking occurred over a grueling six-month period at our regional corporate headquarters.

The primary obstacle we confronted was the sheer complexity of legacy data formats, compounded by an unforgiving deployment deadline. We had to ensure zero downtime for over fifty thousand active global clients while synchronizing disparate legacy databases. Furthermore, midway through the project, several senior specialists had to quarantine due to seasonal health issues, which forced me to shoulder additional architectural duties and coordinate with offshore teams across multiple time zones.

Ultimately, the migration went live seamlessly without a single minute of service disruption. I felt immensely proud not only because the project cut infrastructure overhead by thirty percent, but because it substantiated my leadership capabilities under immense pressure and earned our team formal recognition from executive leadership.
